prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction and experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators, a new class of quantum matter with protected edge states

statement.case_for: Topological insulators remain my first choice because this is a verified physical discovery at the centre, not an instrument or an application. Kane and Mele predicted the quantum spin Hall state and the Z2 classification in 2005, and Molenkamp's group observed the quantized edge conduction in HgTe quantum wells in 2007, a case where theory and experiment together revealed a new state of matter in a solid. It has been reproduced for nearly two decades in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and bulk 3D materials, and angle-resolved photoemission, which is exactly the link between calculation and measured spectra that I value, gave direct evidence for the 3D case. The concept is now part of standard electronic-structure theory, and first-principles codes routinely compute topological invariants and surface states for real materials, so theory and experiment agree quantitatively. The interpretation has been stable, which answers my usual questions about robustness and independent confirmation. The opening ballots show that this is not only my view: Bernhard ranked it second, and the maturity assessments from colleagues converge on 'confirmed and arguably overdue'.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The three-name cap and the credited names leave out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose HgTe proposal made the Molenkamp experiment possible, and the 3D topological insulator contributors (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Hasan, Cava and others). Zhang's death and the 3D history make any trio contestable, and the Kane-Mele graphene mechanism itself is too weak to be observed there, so the experimental realisation rests on a proposal by others. There is also lineage with the 2016 prize for topological phase transitions and topological phases, and the practical benefit is still prospective, which Eva Olsson rightly weighs. If the committee decides that the discovery cannot be credited fairly, B038 or the clock prize are the strongest fallbacks.

responses.point: Bernhard ranked KPZ first and topological insulators second, noting that the topological insulator theory is clean and general and reorganised condensed-matter physics, but that the credited set is contentious because Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore and Hasan are outside it, and that it follows the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I agree on the contested attribution and I do not think it can be dissolved, only argued. My answer is that the prize can be framed around the quantum spin Hall effect as a predicted and then observed phenomenon, which is what Kane and Mele (prediction) and Molenkamp (observation) are credited for, without claiming that every contributor is covered. On the 2016 overlap I am less worried than you: that prize rewarded topological phase transitions and the quantum Hall-type phases, whereas time-reversal-invariant topological insulators are a distinct class that was only found in 2005 to 2008. I find KPZ elegant, but with Parisi outside the credited set and the exact solutions credited elsewhere, I cannot see it being more robustly attributed than topological insulators.

responses.point: Eva ranked topological insulators seventh because the attribution is spread across several communities, Zhang is deceased and Bernevig and Hughes are not credited, and because applications are not yet established, which weighs on the benefit criterion. She put twisted bilayer graphene first and MgO tunnel magnetoresistance third.
responses.response: Your attribution concern is the fair one and I have conceded it above. On benefit, I would say that the statutory emphasis is on the discovery, and the discovery here is a new state of matter that has changed how we classify and compute materials, even if devices are still prospective. We share more than the rankings suggest: I also ranked twisted bilayer graphene fourth and I like it for the same reason as you, but I would want the pairing mechanism and the role of disorder and twist-angle inhomogeneity to be better settled, and I would want the credit for Cao and for Dean's encapsulation work to be resolved before I put it ahead. On MgO tunnelling, I ranked it second, but your point that it is a split between two discoveries and close to the 2007 GMR prize persuades me that it is a weaker prize than I first thought.

responses.point: Göran ranked circuit QED first, but placed topological insulators seventh, noting strong independent confirmation in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and 3D materials with ARPES, that recognition is arguably overdue, but that Zhang's death and the exclusion of Bernevig and Hughes complicate fairness, and he deferred to condensed-matter colleagues.
responses.response: Thank you for deferring, and for stating the confirmation and timing points so plainly, since I think they carry most of the weight. As the condensed-matter voice I will say that the fairness issue is real, but it affects the choice of three names and not the existence of the discovery. I do take seriously your point on the closeness of circuit QED to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits; the same lineage argument is the one I would use against my own ballot with the 2016 prize, and I think it is weaker there because the physics (band topology in time-reversal-symmetric insulators) is distinct, whereas circuit QED builds on the same Josephson-circuit platform that was just honoured.

responses.point: Stefan ranked optical lattice clocks first, arguing that they changed what can be measured at the 10^-18 level, that the result was demonstrated experimentally and reproduced by many laboratories, and that Katori and Ye form a clean two-person pairing.
responses.response: I accept that the clocks have the cleanest attribution of any candidate on the shortlist and that the independent reproducibility is exemplary, which are the criteria I normally push on. It is the strongest challenger to my preference, and it is my second alternative. My hesitation is only about where the central discovery lies: it is a superb measurement technology, and I would like the committee to be explicit about whether a new precision capability, rather than a new phenomenon, is what the prize should recognise this year. I am outside my own field here and will defer to Eva Lindroth and you on whether the second redefinition and the fundamental-physics tests already amount to a discovery of nature.

uncertainties: Whether a fair, defensible three-person credit exists for topological insulators given Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang (deceased) and the 3D contributors, and whether a split with a different credited set would be better.
Whether the 2016 prize on topological phases makes a topological insulator prize look like repetition to the wider community.
Whether the committee prefers a new state of matter (topological insulators, twisted bilayer graphene) or a precision-measurement capability (optical lattice clocks) as this year's emphasis.
For twisted bilayer graphene, whether the pairing mechanism and the credit for Cao and for Dean's work will be sufficiently settled to rank it above topological insulators.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I have no direct collaboration or institutional tie to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp or to the credited names of the alternatives; my work in electronic-structure theory and spin dynamics is field-adjacent to topological materials and magnetic tunnel junctions, which is a matter of expertise and not a conflict.
